news_summary: Scientists have advanced superconductor technology by enhancing strength through innovative use of “empty space.”
news_summary_fr: Les scientifiques ont fait progresser la technologie des supraconducteurs en améliorant leur résistance grâce à une utilisation innovante de « l'espace vide ».
news_summary_es: Los científicos han logrado avances en la tecnología de los superconductores al aumentar su resistencia mediante un uso innovador del «espacio vacío».

articles.title: Scientists just made a superconductor stronger using “empty space”
articles.summary: Researchers have demonstrated that quantum fluctuations in supposedly empty space can strengthen superconductivity, raising the transition temperature of an ultrathin material by as much as 5.4%. The discovery opens the possibility of using specially engineered vacuum environments to control quantum materials without direct contact or external driving.
articles.content:
Researchers have demonstrated for the first time that quantum fluctuations in a vacuum can strengthen superconductivity, opening a new path for controlling unusual states of matter.

The study, published in Nature, was led by Profs. Changgan Zeng and Guanghui Cheng of the University of Science and Technology of China of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The collaboration also included Prof. Qingdong Jiang of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Prof. Frank Wilczek of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and other researchers.

Empty Space Is Not Truly Empty

In everyday language, a vacuum may sound like completely empty space. Quantum physics paints a very different picture.

According to quantum electrodynamics and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, even the lowest energy state is never perfectly still. Virtual particles continually appear and disappear, producing an ever present background of quantum fluctuations.

These fluctuations are not merely theoretical. Their effects have been observed through well established phenomena such as the Lamb shift, spontaneous emission, and the Casimir effect.

For several years, the teams led by Zeng and Cheng have investigated how these vacuum fluctuations affect condensed matter systems. In an earlier study, the researchers showed that they could directly manipulate vacuum fluctuations by using a magnetic field to reversibly switch the Casimir force between attraction and repulsion.

That result raised a larger question: Could quantum vacuum fluctuations also be used to control macroscopic quantum states?

Turning the Vacuum Into a Control Tool

Jiang's group has approached the same problem from a theoretical perspective, studying how engineered quantum vacuum environments could influence different states of matter.

The researchers introduced the concept of "vacuumronics," in which specially designed vacuum environments are used to control electronic and photonic behavior. That theoretical work helped provide a framework for understanding the superconductivity enhancement observed in the new experiments.

"Vacuum fluctuations in free space are generally too weak to produce observable effects in macroscopic condensed-matter systems," said Prof. Zeng. "To overcome this limitation, we introduced a terahertz split-ring resonator. Such a dark cavity can reshape the electromagnetic environment and substantially amplify vacuum fluctuations."

To test the idea experimentally, the researchers placed the superconductor NbSe2 inside a terahertz dark cavity. This created a coupled system in which the superconducting material interacted with the specially engineered electromagnetic environment inside the cavity.

The team then compared the material's superconducting behavior inside and outside the cavity. The results showed that placing NbSe2 in the cavity significantly increased its superconducting critical temperature, the temperature below which the material enters its superconducting state.

Superconductivity Gets Stronger

"We observed that the critical temperature can increase by up to 5.4% in a six-layer NbSe2 device, while the critical current and critical magnetic field are significantly enhanced near the superconducting transition," said Prof. Cheng. "This represents the first experimental observation of vacuum-fluctuation-enhanced superconductivity."

The researchers conducted a series of control experiments to determine whether the effect could be explained by more conventional changes to the material.

They varied several properties of the setup, including the cavity geometry, characteristic frequency, material thicknesses, dielectric materials, and metallic strips. The results allowed them to rule out explanations involving strain, material degradation, inhomogeneity, and metallic screening effects.

One of the strongest clues came from the relationship between the superconductivity enhancement and the characteristic frequency of the dark cavity. Instead of changing smoothly, the enhancement showed a resonance-like peak at a particular frequency.

"This result, closely tied to the cavity's photonic properties, provides strong experimental evidence of the coupling between the superconducting state and dark-cavity modes," said Prof. Zeng.

Virtual Photons May Explain the Effect

To explain what was happening, Jiang's team and Wilczek developed a theoretical model based on the Ginzburg-Landau framework.

Their interpretation suggests that the superconducting state exchanges virtual photons with the dark cavity. This interaction lowers the energy of the superconducting state, making superconductivity more stable and effectively strengthening it.

"When the characteristic energy of the cavity mode matched the low-energy superconducting fluctuations, the NbSe2 device exhibited resonant enhancement, producing the peak in superconductivity enhancement," said Prof. Jiang.

The result changes the usual way physicists think about the vacuum. Rather than serving only as an empty backdrop, the quantum vacuum can potentially be engineered to influence the behavior of matter itself.

"In most practical physics, the vacuum serves merely as the passive stage on which phenomena play out. This work shows that the background itself can become an actor -- engineered to strengthen superconductivity and reshape the behavior of quantum matter," said Prof. Wilczek.

A New Way To Control Quantum Matter

The approach strengthens superconductivity without directly driving the material with an external energy source. Instead, the researchers reshape the surrounding vacuum environment, providing a noncontact method for influencing a quantum state of matter.

That could eventually make engineered vacuum fluctuations a useful new control mechanism for superconductors and other quantum materials.

"With further optimization of cavity structures and material systems, vacuum-fluctuation coupling may enable more pronounced and widely applicable control of quantum states," said Prof. Zeng.

This discovery opens a new, noncontact method to control quantum materials, potentially impacting future quantum technologies and materials science on a broad scale. articles.personality_title: Scientists strengthen superconductors using engineered empty space
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long known that empty space, or vacuum, is not truly empty. Quantum physics shows that tiny particles and energy fluctuations are always present, even in a vacuum. These quantum fluctuations can influence materials in subtle ways.

**What happened** – A team of researchers from China, the US, and other countries placed a thin superconducting material called NbSe2 inside a special cavity designed to enhance vacuum fluctuations. They found that this setup increased the temperature at which the material becomes superconducting by up to 5.4%. This was the first time anyone showed that vacuum fluctuations could strengthen superconductivity in a real experiment.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it shows a new way to control the properties of quantum materials without touching them or using extra energy. Instead, scientists can change the empty space around the material to make it work better. This could help develop better superconductors and quantum devices in the future.

**What's next step** – Researchers plan to improve the design of the cavities and test other materials. They hope to find stronger effects and use this method to control more quantum states. This could open up new possibilities in electronics and quantum technology.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have found a way to boost superconductivity by shaping the empty space around materials, offering a new tool to control quantum states without direct contact.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques renforcent les supraconducteurs en utilisant l’espace vide modifié
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques savent depuis longtemps que l’espace vide, ou vide quantique, n’est pas vraiment vide. La physique quantique montre que de petites particules et fluctuations d’énergie sont toujours présentes, même dans le vide. Ces fluctuations peuvent influencer subtilement les matériaux.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe de chercheurs de Chine, des États-Unis et d’autres pays a placé un matériau supraconducteur mince appelé NbSe2 dans une cavité spéciale conçue pour amplifier les fluctuations du vide. Ils ont découvert que cette configuration augmentait la température à laquelle le matériau devient supraconducteur jusqu’à 5,4 %. C’est la première fois qu’on montre expérimentalement que les fluctuations du vide peuvent renforcer la supraconductivité.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle révèle une nouvelle manière de contrôler les propriétés des matériaux quantiques sans les toucher ni utiliser d’énergie supplémentaire. Les scientifiques peuvent modifier l’espace vide autour du matériau pour améliorer ses performances. Cela pourrait aider à développer de meilleurs supraconducteurs et dispositifs quantiques.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs prévoient d’améliorer la conception des cavités et d’essayer d’autres matériaux. Ils espèrent obtenir des effets plus forts et utiliser cette méthode pour contrôler davantage d’états quantiques. Cela pourrait ouvrir de nouvelles possibilités en électronique et technologie quantique.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont trouvé un moyen d’augmenter la supraconductivité en modifiant l’espace vide autour des matériaux, offrant un nouvel outil pour contrôler les états quantiques sans contact direct.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos fortalecen superconductores usando espacio vacío diseñado
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos saben que el espacio vacío, o vacío cuántico, no está realmente vacío. La física cuántica muestra que pequeñas partículas y fluctuaciones de energía están siempre presentes, incluso en el vacío. Estas fluctuaciones pueden influir sutilmente en los materiales.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo de investigadores de China, Estados Unidos y otros países colocó un material superconductor delgado llamado NbSe2 dentro de una cavidad especial diseñada para aumentar las fluctuaciones del vacío. Descubrieron que esta configuración elevó la temperatura a la que el material se vuelve superconductor hasta en un 5,4 %. Esta fue la primera vez que se demostró experimentalmente que las fluctuaciones del vacío pueden fortalecer la superconductividad.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque muestra una nueva forma de controlar las propiedades de materiales cuánticos sin tocarlos ni usar energía extra. Los científicos pueden cambiar el espacio vacío alrededor del material para mejorar su funcionamiento. Esto podría ayudar a desarrollar mejores superconductores y dispositivos cuánticos.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores planean mejorar el diseño de las cavidades y probar otros materiales. Esperan encontrar efectos más fuertes y usar este método para controlar más estados cuánticos. Esto podría abrir nuevas posibilidades en electrónica y tecnología cuántica.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los científicos encontraron una forma de aumentar la superconductividad modificando el espacio vacío alrededor de los materiales, ofreciendo una nueva herramienta para controlar estados cuánticos sin contacto directo.
